newsitem.title: USA: U.S. West runoff forecasts expected this week.
newsitem.headline: U.S. West runoff forecasts expected this week.

text.p: The first official forecasts for this year's river runoff in the Pacific Northwest, California and Nevada will be released later this week amid industry expectations the number will be well above normal.
"We weren't prepared for this (rainfall)," said one California-based utility manager. "We seem to be having a 'pineapple connection' of storms from the Pacific."
He and others noted that precipitation in the western U.S. tends to vary between much higher than normal or drought conditions, with those wide swings averaging out over time.
Increased water flows translate into higher hydroelectric power generation, which is often the lowest-cost power source for electric utilities.

"We have seen above-normal conditions for three out of the last four years," noted an hydrologist at Southern California Edison Co. "But before that we had several years of drought. Normal is the arithmatic mean of a lot of dry years and a lot of wet years."
As of late last month, Edison's preliminary forecast was for runoff at its San Joaquin River projects to total 169 percent of normal levels.

Since then, concerns have grown about early runoff as the mountain snowpack is melted by the mild weather and heavy rains that produced widespread flooding in central and northern California over the past week.
But some sources said the outlook for hydroelectric output remains rosy with January and February--generally the region's wettest months--still to come.
A source at the California Department of Water Resources said the state's reservoirs held 120 percent of normal volumes by mid-December, but "god knows where they are now, things are pretty high."
The state agency expects to assess the reservoir total again next week.
"We still have some good accumulation left ahead of us," said Nancy Stephen, head of weather and streamflow forecasting at Bonneville Power Administration (BPA) in Portland, Ore.
In the Northwest, an "early-bird" forecast by the regional River Forecast Center put January-July runoff at 113 percent of normal, but it was made before the latest storm series.
For the previous water year (October 1, 1995 to September 30, 1996) runoff for the Columbia River basin was 139 percent ofnormal.
Industry sources had expected flows to return to more normal levels this year, but now say that looks unlikely.
BPA's Stephen said snowpack for much of the Pacific Northwest is above 100 percent of normal, if not above 200 percent in some cases.
"Given the track we're on now, there is nothing to indicate that (weather patterns) will turn around," she added.
